what: Valaris owns offshore drilling rigs. It operates drillships and semi-submersibles that drill oil and gas wells in deep water, along with jack-up rigs for shallower water, leasing them with crews to oil companies at a daily rate.
customers: International and national oil companies drilling offshore, in the Gulf of Mexico, Brazil, West Africa, the North Sea and the Middle East.
money: Drillships and semi-submersibles for deepwater drilling, at the highest day rates.
Rigs for shallow water, mostly working in the Middle East and North Sea.
moat: The most capable deepwater drillships cost hundreds of millions, take years to build, and essentially none have been ordered in a decade, because the last building cycle bankrupted most of the industry. So supply is fixed while deepwater activity recovers, and Valaris owns a substantial share of the modern fleet.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $206.8M, as rigs are reactivated and upgraded before they can earn — reactivation costs tens of millions per rig.
Seven analysts average a $70.86 target against a $72.77 price, slightly below, which is an unusual signal of caution.
Day rates depend entirely on oil company exploration budgets, which are set annually and cut quickly.
A rig without a contract earns nothing while still costing money to maintain, so utilisation determines everything.
At 16.8 times EV/EBITDA the price is not obviously cheap despite the low price/earnings ratio.
opportunities: Last year’s net margin was 41.5%, and the shares trade at about 6.5 times earnings.
Cash of $599.4M against $1.2B of debt is a far cleaner balance sheet than most offshore drillers carry.
Revenue has grown from $1.6B in 2022 to $2.4B in 2025, as deepwater activity recovered.
No new high-specification drillships have been ordered in a decade, so supply is fixed while demand recovers.
Valaris emerged from restructuring with a modern fleet and much less debt than its history would suggest.
watch: Day rates on new contracts and fleet utilisation. An offshore driller earns rigs working multiplied by the daily rate, and both are disclosed contract by contract.
view: Valaris went through bankruptcy in 2021 along with most of the offshore drilling industry, and what emerged is the interesting part: a modern fleet with $1.2 billion of debt against $599 million of cash. That is a materially cleaner balance sheet than Transocean’s, and in a business where leverage is what kills companies, it is the single most important distinction between offshore drillers.

The industry setup is genuinely favourable. Nobody has ordered a new high-specification drillship in roughly a decade, because no lender will finance one and no board will approve it after what happened last time. Supply is therefore fixed and slowly shrinking as old units are scrapped, while deepwater drilling has recovered because oil companies want long-life, low-decline projects. Fixed supply meeting rising demand is the setup that produces very high day rates, and last year’s 41.5% net margin shows it working.

The negative free cash flow of $207 million needs explaining rather than fearing. Reactivating a cold-stacked rig costs tens of millions and takes months before it earns anything, so a driller expanding its working fleet consumes cash before it generates it. That is investment, not deterioration — but it does mean the cash flow statement understates the earning power of the fleet once contracted.

What gives me pause is the seven analysts averaging a target slightly below the share price, and 16.8 times EV/EBITDA. Analysts rarely publish no upside, and this is a cyclical business at a point in the cycle that already looks good. The cleaner balance sheet makes Valaris the better vehicle for this theme than its more leveraged peers, but the price no longer assumes the cycle is early. Day rates on new contracts are the number that decides it, and they are disclosed rig by rig.
bull: Fixed drillship supply meets recovering deepwater demand, day rates keep rising, and a modern fleet with a clean balance sheet captures it without leverage risk.
bear: Oil companies cut exploration budgets, utilisation falls, and reactivation spending turns out to have been made into a softening market.
